clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia caused by heterozygous variants in TMEM240 on chromosome 1p36.33; unlike many spinocerebellar ataxias it is a conventional point-mutation disorder, not a repeat expansion.
Cognitive impairment — ranging from subtle executive deficits to intellectual disability in early-onset cases — is a hallmark that helps separate it from the purely cerebellar subtypes.
Age at onset is broad, spanning childhood to mid-adult life, with slowly progressive gait ataxia, limb dysmetria and dysarthria.
Extrapyramidal features are characteristic: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting or postural tremor and a parkinsonian appearance in some patients.
Hyporeflexia or areflexia is frequently observed, contrasting with the brisk reflexes seen in several other dominant ataxias.
Brain imaging typically shows cerebellar and vermian atrophy with a relatively preserved brainstem.
First delineated in a French kindred; intrafamilial variability in severity and cognitive burden is wide.
Diagnosis relies on targeted gene or ataxia-panel/exome sequencing because the causative change is a missense (or start-loss) variant rather than an expanded repeat.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA21 arises from heterozygous variants in TMEM240, which encodes a small transmembrane protein of incompletely defined function that is strongly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells and more widely in the developing and mature brain. The disease-associated missense and start-loss variants are thought to act through a dominant mechanism that disturbs Purkinje-cell homeostasis and cerebellar cortical circuitry, producing slowly progressive cerebellar degeneration; because the protein also appears important during neurodevelopment, cognitive impairment and extrapyramidal signs accompany the ataxia and give the subtype its distinctive multidomain phenotype. As no nucleotide repeat is involved, genetic anticipation is not a feature.
additionalDifferentials: SCA13 (KCNC3) — dominant ataxia with cognitive impairment and, in some, childhood onset
SCA19/22 (KCND3) — ataxia with cognitive and occasional extrapyramidal features
SCA2 and SCA3 — subtypes in which parkinsonism can dominate the picture
SCA17 (TBP) — ataxia with cognitive decline, psychiatric change and chorea
Autosomal recessive early-onset ataxias when presentation is in childhood
Wilson disease — young-onset ataxia combined with extrapyramidal signs (a treatable mimic)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to demonstrate cerebellar and vermian atrophy and exclude structural lesions
Formal neuropsychological assessment to characterise and monitor the cognitive profile
Targeted TMEM240 sequencing or a hereditary-ataxia gene panel / exome
Dedicated repeat-expansion testing to exclude the common repeat-based subtypes
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin plus an acquired-ataxia screen where diagnosis is unclear
Family segregation analysis with formal genetic counselling
redFlags: Rapidly progressive course or prominent bulbar dysfunction suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Severe or early cognitive decline disproportionate to the motor deficit
Marked parkinsonism, dystonia or new movement disorder prompting re-evaluation
reference.prognosis: The course is slowly progressive over decades and many patients retain independent walking for a prolonged period, although cumulative cognitive and extrapyramidal involvement adds to disability. Life expectancy is often close to normal.
pitfalls: Attributing the cognitive impairment to a primary dementia or psychiatric disorder rather than the ataxia syndrome
Assuming a repeat-expansion mechanism and stopping the work-up after negative repeat panels
Overlooking the parkinsonian features and mislabelling the patient as having idiopathic Parkinson disease
Mistaking the hyporeflexia for a primary peripheral neuropathy
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
